agentCan: Implement the authorization-code (and PKCE) flow with correct refresh-rotation persistence
Generate per-instance application setup instructions for Self-Managed customers
Advise the narrowest workable scope set (avoiding the all-powerful api scope where possible)

approval.trigger: No GitLab review exists in the documentation: no approval, submission, vetting, marketplace, or listing step for OAuth applications. The application works as soon as it is saved; the only consent event is the end user approving the requested scopes on the authorize page. (For Admin-area instance-wide apps, an admin can mark the app 'trusted', which skips the user authorization step entirely.)

blockers.detail: An application is registered ON an instance. Your gitlab.com registration does not exist on a customer's Self-Managed or Dedicated instance; supporting self-hosted customers means an application must be created on each such instance, with per-instance Application ID/Secret pairs.
blockers.howToClear: Build per-instance credential storage and a customer-admin setup guide; treat self-hosted onboarding as a separate flow from gitlab.com.
blockers.title: Per-instance fragmentation

blockers.detail: The headline scope, api, 'grants complete read/write access to the API, including all groups and projects, the container registry, the dependency proxy, and the package registry'. Narrower options exist (read_api, read_user, read_repository, write_repository, registry scopes, openid/profile/email), but there is no per-project granularity, and the same list contains dangerous scopes (sudo, admin_mode).
blockers.howToClear: Request read_api or repository scopes when they suffice; treat api as a deliberate, disclosed decision.
blockers.title: Coarse, powerful scopes

blockers.detail: Refreshing 'invalidates the existing access token AND refresh token' and issues new ones. A client that fails to persist the replacement refresh token breaks the connection on the next cycle.
blockers.howToClear: Persist the new refresh token atomically on every refresh, exactly like Atlassian's and Bitbucket's rotation models.
blockers.title: Refresh invalidates both tokens

sources.label: Configure GitLab as an OAuth 2.0 identity provider (application types, scopes, token expiry)
OAuth 2.0 identity provider API (flows, PKCE, refresh invalidation)

tested: Read-only verification: application types, creation steps, scope table, and token behavior were checked against GitLab's official documentation. Transparency note: docs.gitlab.com was blocked to the research reader, so the identical official documentation was read via the /help pages GitLab ships inside its instances; canonical docs.gitlab.com URLs are cited. No application was created, nothing submitted.

alternatives: Group-owned application (scoped to one group; enables group SAML SSO redirection for OAuth apps)
Instance-wide application (Self-Managed only, created by an admin; can be marked trusted so the user authorization step is skipped)
flavor.recommended: A user-owned OAuth 2 application in your own GitLab.com account, using the authorization code flow with PKCE
flavor.why: GitLab's API docs state the authorization code flow 'requires application to be registered first via the /user_settings/applications page in your user's account': one vendor registration, and each customer authorizes with their own GitLab account. PKCE is documented as 'most secure, recommended for both client and server apps' (a plain authorization-code flow is the recommended option for secure server-side apps; a Device Authorization Grant also exists).

humanMust: Create the application in your GitLab account and capture the Secret at creation (it is stored hashed and only available immediately after creating)
For self-hosted customers: their instance admin (or a user there) creates the per-instance application
name: GitLab
nuances: Access tokens expire after two hours by default (7200 seconds); on Self-Managed/Dedicated, admins can configure the maximum token lifetime.
Standard OAuth tokens cannot authenticate directly to the container registry or package registries; they can only manage those resources via the registry APIs.
Implicit and Resource Owner Password flows are gone from the current supported list (the OAuth 2.1 draft omits both); some older instance mirrors still list ROPC, so expect version skew in the wild.
A token with read_repository/write_repository works as the password for git over HTTPS with username 'oauth2'.
Deleting an application deletes all of its grants and tokens; renewing a secret breaks the app until credentials are updated everywhere.
prerequisites: A GitLab.com account (for the SaaS path)
Your redirect URI (HTTPS for production; HTTP allowed for development)

steps.detail: Avatar > Edit profile > Access > Applications > Add new application. (Group-owned: Group > Settings > Applications. Instance-wide: Admin > Applications, Self-Managed only.)
steps.title: Add a new application

steps.detail: Enter Name, Redirect URI (SSL recommended), and select Scopes (see the scope table; prefer narrower scopes over api when they suffice).
steps.title: Set name, redirect URI, and scopes

steps.detail: Save. GitLab returns the Application ID (client ID) and Secret. Secrets are stored hashed and are only available immediately after creation: copy and vault it now. A Renew secret function exists, but renewing prevents the application from functioning until credentials are updated.
steps.title: Save and capture the Application ID and Secret

steps.detail: Redirect users to /oauth/authorize (client_id, redirect_uri, response_type=code, state, scope); the authorize page asks the user to approve the requested scopes. Exchange the code at /oauth/token (client secret for the plain code flow; no secret with PKCE). Call the API with Authorization: Bearer. Users can review and revoke grants anytime under their Authorized applications.
steps.title: Implement the flow

steps.detail: Refresh tokens work even after the access token expires, but each refresh invalidates the old access AND refresh tokens and issues new ones. Persist the replacement every time.
steps.title: Handle refresh rotation correctly

tagline: GitHub-class self-serve OAuth with zero review, but with a SaaS catch: your app registration lives on one instance, so every self-hosted customer needs their own. Scopes are coarse, crowned by an 'api' scope that grants nearly everything.

time.active: ~5 min of form work + ~1-2 hrs of standard flow code
time.total: Same day on GitLab.com; self-hosted customers add a per-instance setup step
